rows.stem: In an A.P., if \(a_{14} - a_8 = 24\), then the common difference of the A.P. is
rows.solution:
\(a_{14} - a_8 = (a + 13d) - (a + 7d) = 6d\).

So \(6d = 24\) and \(d = 4\). The equation is linear in d, so there is exactly one value, not two.

This is option (B) \(4\).

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: If sum and product of zeroes of a polynomial are \((-3)\) and \((-2)\) respectively, then a polynomial is
rows.solution:
A quadratic with sum of zeroes S and product P is a non-zero multiple of \(x^2 - Sx + P\). Here \(S = -3\) and \(P = -2\), so it is a multiple of \(x^2 + 3x - 2\).

Multiplying by \(-1\) gives \(-x^2 - 3x + 2\). Check: sum \(= -\dfrac{-3}{-1} = -3\) and product \(= \dfrac{2}{-1} = -2\). (The choice \(x^2 + 3x + 2\) has the right sum but product 2.)

This is option (B) \(-x^2 - 3x + 2\).

rows.stem: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 10 cm is \(\dfrac{55}{3}\,\text{cm}^2\). The value of central angle is
rows.solution:
Area of a sector \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times \pi r^2\):

\(\dfrac{55}{3} = \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10 \times 10 = \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times \dfrac{2200}{7}\).

So \(\theta = \dfrac{55}{3} \times \dfrac{7}{2200} \times 360^\circ = 21^\circ\), which is option (D) \(21^\circ\).

rows.stem: For acute angles A and B, if \(\sec(2A - B) = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}(A + B) = 2\), then find the values of A and B.
rows.solution:
\(\sec(2A - B) = \sqrt{2} = \sec 45^\circ\), so \(2A - B = 45^\circ\) ... (1)

\(\operatorname{cosec}(A + B) = 2 = \operatorname{cosec} 30^\circ\), so \(A + B = 30^\circ\) ... (2)

Adding (1) and (2): \(3A = 75^\circ\), so \(A = 25^\circ\). Then from (2), \(B = 30^\circ - 25^\circ = 5^\circ\).

So \(A = 25^\circ\) and \(B = 5^\circ\).

\(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

\(\dfrac{2\cos 30^\circ - \cot^3 60^\circ}{\tan 30^\circ} = \dfrac{2 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\)

Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\): \(= 3 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(4 - 2\sqrt{5}\) is an irrational number given that \(\sqrt{5}\) is irrational.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(4 - 2\sqrt{5}\) is rational. Then \(4 - 2\sqrt{5} = \dfrac{a}{b}\), where a and b are integers and \(b \neq 0\).

Rearranging, \(\sqrt{5} = \dfrac{4b - a}{2b}\). The right side is a ratio of integers, so it is rational; but \(\sqrt{5}\) is irrational. This is a contradiction.

So the assumption is wrong, and \(4 - 2\sqrt{5}\) is irrational.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: Use graphical method to solve the system of linear equations : \(y = -3\) and \(x + 2y = 4\).
rows.solution:
\(y = -3\) is the horizontal line through \((0, -3)\), parallel to the x-axis.

Points on \(x + 2y = 4\), that is \(x = 4 - 2y\):

| \(x\) | 0 | 4 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 2 | 0 | \(-3\) |

Plot these points and draw the line through them, and draw the line \(y = -3\) on the same axes. The two lines meet at \((10, -3)\).

The solution is \(x = 10\), \(y = -3\). (Check: \(10 + 2(-3) = 4\).)

Write everything in sines and cosines:

LHS \(= \left(1 + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\right) = \dfrac{\sin\theta + \cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta} \times \dfrac{\cos\theta + \sin\theta + 1}{\cos\theta}\)

The numerators have the form \((u - 1)(u + 1)\) with \(u = \sin\theta + \cos\theta\), so

\(= \dfrac{(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 - 1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\)

\(= 2 =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: By selling an article for ₹ 48, a trader loses as much percent as half of the cost price of the article. Calculate the cost price and loss amount of the article.
rows.solution:
Let the cost price of the article be ₹ x. The loss percent is \(\dfrac{x}{2}\), so

Loss \(= \dfrac{x}{2}\%\) of \(x = \dfrac{x}{2} \times \dfrac{x}{100} = \dfrac{x^2}{200}\).

Selling price \(=\) cost price \(-\) loss: \(48 = x - \dfrac{x^2}{200}\).

Multiplying by 200: \(9600 = 200x - x^2\), that is \(x^2 - 200x + 9600 = 0\).

\((x - 120)(x - 80) = 0\), so \(x = 120\) or \(x = 80\). Both are possible.

When the cost price is ₹ 120, the loss is \(120 - 48 =\) ₹ 72 (a loss of 60%, half of 120).

When the cost price is ₹ 80, the loss is \(80 - 48 =\) ₹ 32 (a loss of 40%, half of 80).
